Once they were legitimate protection for individuals against large corporations. You could easily file a patent for very little out of pocket money and have reasonable access to courts in order to defend your property rights. That is no longer the case.

Almost no one outside of large corporations or individuals with an unhealthy love affair with their invention even file patents anymore. It is now just a bunch of corps filing patents on every little thing they can think of. This keeps any upstarts from every gaining traction and fills their arsenal to counter sue when they steal other corporations patents. All the big companies square off with this cold war stare down as they keep creating new patents. The cost to create is through the roof so that only the big companies can afford it. The cost to defend is even worse.

How do we fix it? Well, there are a few things that would help a great deal.

  1. The patent follows the individuals, not the company. No organization should be allowed to own a patent.

  2. Stricter rules on who can be on the patent application. If you are some dip shit MBA then the chances are you did nothing to create that intellectual property.

  3. Streamline and reduce costs for individual filers. If you are a single person filing then you should get a significant discount on the application costs.

  4. Shorten the patent life time. In today's speed of technology, patent life should be 10 years, 15 tops.

  5. If an individual is let go or leaves a company he can extend all patent IP that he has his name on to his new employer.

Other people have already hit on the abuse topic, so I'm going to skip there to another one that many people don't consider: simultaneous discovery. The problem with claiming rights to something is that very often people, completely independently, invent the exact same thing. Maybe the most famous example is calculus. Newton is probably given the most credit, but Liebnitz also discovered calculus at damn near the exact same time. And they're just the big two - others were also discovering it about the same time.

Today there are more than 7 billion people in the world and millions of inventors, scientists, researchers, and so on. People are constantly discovering things -even incredibly esoteric things- simultaneously. I think in this regard intellectual property rights are really working like a ball and chain on progress. I think this is the most significant issue. As our population intellectually evolves intellectual property rights are going to become more and more arbitrary. The solution? So far as I can see, there is no particularly good one. It makes our IP laws rather damned if you do, and damned if you don't. But I suppose for now at least that we're less damned if we do than if we don't.
